name: Guardian cryptic crossword, Penguin book 5 No 18

book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 5

entries.clue: Any activity, such as a dance for the disabled? (4,4)

blocks.note: the formal dance with a band and a floor, the kind you are invited to
game means lame, the sense kept alive in a game leg

annotation.surface: Some pastime or other laid on for disabled people, a dance perhaps.
annotation.walkthrough: Game meaning lame survives almost nowhere except the phrase 'a game leg', which is why the second half of the answer hides so well. The definition leans on the idiom: a different ball game is a different matter entirely.
annotation.definitionFit: In the idiom 'a whole new ball game' the phrase stands for any undertaking at all, not just a sport played with a ball.

entries.clue: Reduction in total protection of legionary (6)

indicators.note: 'In' puts one thing inside another, so the word before it goes bodily into the middle of the word after.

blocks.note: the total at the foot of a column of figures is its sum
a cut in spending is a reduction

annotation.surface: Less money being spent on keeping a Roman soldier safe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reduction in total' reads as one idea, a shrinking budget, which is why its three words do not look like separate pieces of wordplay. The shield it names is the tall curved rectangle of the shield-wall, not a round buckler.
annotation.definitionFit: A scutum is the shield a Roman legionary carried, so the phrase names his standard protection rather than armour in general.

entries.clue: Get over medical officer’s U-turn, perhaps (8)

indicators.note: 'Perhaps' offers what stands before it as one possible arrangement rather than the fixed one, which is a loose way of asking for a shuffle and the only instruction here.

blocks.note: a medical officer is MO in the services, the possessive s stays in the mix, and the manoeuvre adds its own five letters

annotation.surface: A doctor changing his mind, and the trouble of getting past it.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole of 'U-turn' is raw material, letters and all, rather than an instruction to turn anything round: the manoeuvre is being spelt out, not performed. MO is the forces' medical officer, and his apostrophe-s goes into the pile with him.
annotation.definitionFit: To surmount an obstacle is to get over it, the same figurative climb whether the thing in the way is a wall or a difficulty.

entries.clue: Child is below insect (6)

blocks.note: inf. is the footnote's short form of Latin infra, below — 'see inf.' sends you down the page
the setters' insect of choice, three letters and always at work

annotation.surface: A youngster standing underneath a creepy-crawly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Below' is not telling you where to put anything: it is the footnote abbreviation inf., from Latin infra, and it supplies half the letters. In an across clue nothing could sit below anything in the first place.
annotation.definitionFit: An infant is a child at its youngest, the word the law and the nursery both use for one not yet grown.

entries.clue: Some jeering about awfully prurient supplier of gin (7,4)

indicators.note: Some of a word is a part of it and not the lot, so the rest of its letters are dropped before anything else happens.
A thing placed about another is wrapped round it, so the letters just taken go outside what comes next.
Something done awfully is done badly, and letters handled badly do not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: three letters taken in order from the front of the word
the eight letters of the word re-set

annotation.surface: A bout of mockery aimed at a very dirty-minded drinks merchant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Awfully prurient' looks like the surface's insult and is the fodder; the shuffle then sits inside three letters lifted from 'jeering', split one in front and two behind, which is what makes them so hard to see. Gin's name is a shortening of genever, Dutch for juniper.
annotation.definitionFit: Gin is distilled with juniper berries and named after them, so the tree that grows them supplies the one flavour that makes gin gin.

entries.clue: Fish taken for a song? Could be a snag (5)

blocks.note: the haul a boat lands, counted in crates on the quay
a round for several voices, each coming in as the one before reaches the second line
the hidden condition in an offer that sounds too good

annotation.surface: Fish bought dirt cheap, which may turn out to have something wrong with it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taken for a song' is the idiom for bought at a giveaway price, and the clue quietly splits it: the fish are taken, and the song stands on its own. A third sense follows it, the drawback hidden in a bargain.
annotation.definitionFit: A catch is the fish landed, a catch is a round sung in parts, and a catch is the drawback hidden in a tempting offer.

entries.clue: Devon clinic backs tax on single family (9)

indicators.note: A word that backs in an across clue is read the other way along the row, right to left, so the letters beside it come out reversed.

blocks.note: VAT is the tax added to almost everything bought in Britain, written here the other way round
one, the single thing, is the Roman numeral I
the line you come of is your stock, as in good farming stock

annotation.surface: A West Country clinic supporting a levy on one-parent households.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backs' reads as supports, which is what a clinic might do to a policy, and does the crossword job of turning the tax round. 'Single family' is a real phrase on the surface and two separate pieces underneath it.
annotation.definitionFit: Tavistock is the market town on the western edge of Dartmoor in Devon, and the Tavistock is the name of Britain's best-known psychiatric clinic.

entries.clue: Sort of college, little one, with eater? (9)

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition a noun phrase: the setter is naming the compound the word lives in, an electoral college, rather than offering a synonym for the word itself.

indicators.note: To sort a handful of letters is to put them in whatever order you choose, so what follows is raw material rather than a word.

blocks.note: the little one of the two ways to write the word just used: coll. is the abbreviation on the letterhead
the word taken at face value, all five letters

annotation.surface: A small college of one kind or another, with somebody to feed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sort of college' does both jobs at once: it defines the answer, and read again 'sort' is the instruction to rearrange. 'Little one' then asks for the short form of the word standing in front of it.
annotation.definitionFit: An electoral college is the body of people whose votes actually choose a president, so 'sort of college' names the word that goes in front of it.

entries.clue: Quick blow to the instincts (5)

blocks.note: a rap on the knuckles is a sharp blow
Freud's id is the unconscious store of instinct and appetite, sitting under the ego

annotation.surface: A quick punch aimed at where somebody's instincts live.
annotation.walkthrough: Freud divided the mind into id, ego and superego, and the id is the store of instinct and appetite — two letters the crossword never tires of. 'Quick' is an adjective, so the answer is one too.
annotation.definitionFit: Quick and rapid are a plain adjective pair — a rapid reply is a quick one — with no shade of meaning between them.

entries.clue: Heeding Lent when converted like the Buddha (11)

indicators.note: Something converted has been turned into something else, so the letters in front are to be made into a different word.

blocks.note: eleven letters, exactly the count the grid asks for

annotation.surface: Someone who took Lent seriously and came out of it a changed person.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Converted' carries its religious sense on the surface — a convert is what Lent might make of you — and its mechanical one in the wordplay. The Buddha's name is a title rather than a name: it means the one who woke up.
annotation.definitionFit: The Buddha is 'the enlightened one', the title meaning exactly that, so the adjective describes him before it describes anybody else.

entries.clue: Girl turning head of Mary Lamb (6)

indicators.note: A thing turning comes round to face the other way, so the letters it is applied to are written out in reverse.

blocks.note: the head of the name is its first two letters, MA, and they come round the other way
Charles Lamb signed his essays Elia, a name borrowed from an Italian clerk he had worked beside

annotation.surface: A girl turning the head of Mary's lamb.
annotation.walkthrough: Mary's lamb is the nursery rhyme; Charles Lamb the essayist is the other one, and he published as Elia in the London Magazine from 1820. 'Head' asks for the front of the word, not for its first letter alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Amelia is a girl's name, and 'Girl' is the setter's standing way of asking for one without saying which.

entries.clue: Irrespective of other force, the Queen replaces me for opening (8)

indicators.note: What replaces something stands where it stood, so one set of letters is lifted out and the other put into the gap.

blocks.note: the opening letter of a word is its initial, and that whole word is what is being worked on
me spoken as the subject is I, a single letter
Elizabeth Regina, the cypher stamped on every postbox of her reign

annotation.surface: A monarch stepping into somebody's place at the start of proceedings.
annotation.walkthrough: Three of the letters worked on are I, which is what makes the swap hard to place — it is the middle one that goes. 'Opening' names a whole word here, not a first letter to be taken off something else.
annotation.definitionFit: An inertial path is the one a body keeps when nothing else acts on it, so the phrase describes motion owing nothing to any other force.

entries.clue: Instrument beheaded is still with us (6)

indicators.note: To behead a thing is to take the head off it, and a word's head is the letter standing at its front.

blocks.note: the navigator's instrument for measuring the sun's angle above the horizon
this S stands at the head of that instrument's name and is the letter struck off

annotation.surface: An instrument that has lost its head and is somehow still around.
annotation.walkthrough: A sextant still rides in the lifeboat as a backup for when the satellites fail, so the surface's survivor and the wordplay's instrument are the same object. 'Beheaded' costs one letter, not a whole top half.
annotation.definitionFit: Something extant has not died out: the manuscripts extant are the ones that have come down to us and can still be read.

entries.clue: Whisky money for black food (3-5)

blocks.note: rye is the American whiskey distilled from that grain instead of from barley
bread is the old slang for cash, out of the same drawer as dough

annotation.surface: Drink money being spent on something dark to eat.
annotation.walkthrough: Bread and dough are both slang for money, and the setter has picked the one that is also something to eat. The whisky is the American rye, not the Scotch the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Rye bread is dark brown to black beside a wheat loaf, and black bread is the standard English name for it.

entries.clue: Water-carrier keeps silence with German agreement in a piece of drill (4-6)

indicators.note: To keep a thing is to hold on to it, and what a word holds sits inside it rather than beside it.

blocks.note: the thing you fetch water in, a pail with a handle
the noise made for silence, spelt the way a library notice spells it
ja is yes in German

annotation.surface: A water-carrier keeping quiet and nodding along in German during square-bashing.
annotation.walkthrough: Drill is cloth as well as parade-ground practice: a stout cotton twill, and this garment is cut from it. Two short scraps go in together, which is why the carrier's six letters come apart so unevenly.
annotation.definitionFit: Drill is the hard-wearing cotton twill that tropical kit is made from, so a garment cut from it is literally a piece of drill.

entries.clue: Handled viewers from long street (10)

indicators.note: A thing made from a set of parts is built out of them in whatever order suits, so the words after it are letters rather than a phrase.

blocks.note: ten letters, the length the grid wants

annotation.surface: Opera glasses that came from a long road somewhere.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Handled' reads as dealt with, the way you handle a customer, and means fitted with a handle. 'From' is the only word asking for a rearrangement, which is about as quiet as an anagram signal gets.
annotation.definitionFit: Lorgnettes are eyeglasses on a stick, raised to the eyes rather than worn, so both halves of the definition are literally true of them.

entries.clue: Set to mature pointlessly (5)

indicators.note: Without a point means without one of the compass's, so the letter that names a direction is dropped.

blocks.note: what a child is told to do: grow up
W is west on the compass card, and it is the point taken away

annotation.surface: Telling somebody to grow up, for all the good it will do.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pointlessly' does not mean the growing up is futile; it means the compass point comes out. 'Set' is a noun here, a set of people, though the clue reads as an instruction to somebody.
annotation.definitionFit: A set and a group are the same collection of things considered together: a set of friends is a group of them.

entries.clue: Guardian’s job? Not democracy, or else I return my oil (8,4)

indicators.note: 'Or else' holds out the other possibility, so the letters that follow are to be taken in some order other than the one they come in.

blocks.note: twelve letters, counting the one-letter word, which is exactly the grid's count

annotation.surface: A threat to hand back somebody's oil unless the newspaper does its job.
annotation.walkthrough: A guardian rules while the heir is under age, a minority in the legal sense, so the question mark covers a definition that is also a dig at the paper. Araucaria set this for the Guardian itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Rule by a minority is the opposite of democracy, and a guardian's job is exactly that: ruling on someone's behalf through their minority.

entries.clue: Electrical device that summarises study for the less intelligent? (9)

blocks.note: to con a thing is to learn it by heart, the old verb for studying a page closely
dense means slow-witted, so the comparative is the one further along that scale

annotation.surface: A gadget that boils long texts down for people who cannot follow them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Con' for study is an old sense crosswords keep alive — you con a part before you act it — and has nothing to do with swindling. Calling the dim dense is the same metaphor as calling them thick.
annotation.definitionFit: A condenser is the old name for a capacitor, and a condenser is also whatever condenses a text, so both halves of the definition hold.

entries.clue: Fellow player makes anagrams (4-4)

blocks.note: the man beside you in the side, playing for the same result
on the surface a hobby; in the answer a description of its own two halves, which are the same four letters in different orders

annotation.surface: A fellow in the side who does anagrams for fun.
annotation.walkthrough: There is no fodder anywhere to shuffle: the clue is telling you that the answer's two halves are anagrams of each other, and that is the whole of the wordplay. Each half runs to four letters, as the enumeration says.
annotation.definitionFit: A team-mate is a fellow player, the person on your own side rather than one of the opposition.

entries.clue: See 7
Supplier of tickets for assorted clean vegetables in carrier (6,6)

indicators.note: An assorted boxful is one with no order to it, so the letters that follow are to be taken in any arrangement.
What is in a thing sits inside it, so the letters just made go into the middle of the word after.

blocks.note: a tray is what a waiter carries the drinks on
vegetables shorten to veg, and those eight letters are re-set

annotation.surface: A ticket seller whose basket is full of assorted washed vegetables.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is not the words as printed: 'vegetables' has to be shortened to veg first, and only then do the letters fit inside the carrier. A tray carries things, which is all the clue means by carrier.
annotation.definitionFit: A travel agency is the shop that sells you the tickets and books the hotel, so supplying tickets is what it does over the counter.

entries.clue: Gold enclosed in tree by fretful Shakespearean beast (10)

indicators.note: Letters put in a word go inside it, with what is left of it standing on either side.

blocks.note: the evergreen of the plantation, four letters and a setter's favourite
or is gold in heraldry, the tincture of a gold field
pent is shut in, as in pent-up feelings that cannot get out

annotation.surface: Gold shut up inside a tree, beside an anxious animal out of Shakespeare.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Enclosed' looks like the instruction and is a piece of the answer instead — 'in' does the enclosing. The Ghost in Hamlet says his tale would make the hair stand up 'like quills upon the fretful porpentine'.
annotation.definitionFit: Porpentine is Shakespeare's spelling of porcupine, and fretful is the very word his Ghost attaches to the creature.

entries.clue: Ran away with new desk — bad! (10)

indicators.note: Something new is not as it was, so the letters beside the word are to be set down in a fresh order.

blocks.note: the four letters of the furniture, re-set
an addled egg is a bad one, gone off inside the shell

annotation.surface: Someone made off with a new desk, which is a bad business.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes 'bad' read as a verdict on the theft rather than as six of the ten letters. Skedaddled came out of the American Civil War and still sounds like a joke word on this side of the Atlantic.
annotation.definitionFit: To skedaddle is to run away in a hurry, and the tense matches: they skedaddled is they ran away.

entries.clue: Hothead changed 25 with a brown shirt (9)

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and 'a brown shirt' names a person: the Brownshirts were Hitler's SA stormtroopers, so the setter defines the adjective by the men it describes.

indicators.note: What has been changed is no longer as it was, so the letters named alongside are to be rebuilt in another order.

blocks.note: the head of HOT, its first letter
the answer at 25 across, whose eight letters join that one in the mix

annotation.surface: A hot-tempered man who changed sides and put on a brown shirt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hothead' is one word on the page and two instructions underneath it, since the head of 'hot' is its first letter. The Brownshirts were the SA, the party's street fighters, uniformed in brown and broken by Hitler in 1934.
annotation.definitionFit: A Brownshirt was one of Hitler's SA men, named for the uniform, so anything belonging to them is Hitlerian.

entries.clue: Bath robe gives some excitement (5)

indicators.note: Giving some of a thing hands over a part and keeps the rest, so only a run of the letters in front is wanted.

blocks.note: five letters running on unbroken across the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: A dressing gown from the spa town that people find thrilling.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital B lets Bath look like the spa city, and splitting 'bathrobe' into two words hides the run of letters entirely. 'Gives' reads as the sentence's own verb and is half the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A throb is a surge of feeling you can feel in the body — a throb of excitement — so the noun names excitement as a beat.

entries.clue: Unexciting river of 7 or... (4)

definitions.note: The two words define separately: the answer is the adjective meaning unexciting, and it is also the name of a river, which is what 'river' is there to tell you.

blocks.note: the answer at 7 down, four letters to be re-set

annotation.surface: A river with nothing exciting about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The instruction to shuffle is in the next clue: 'cooked' at 23 down serves both halves of the pair, which is what the dots are for. The Tame runs through Birmingham and joins the Trent.
annotation.definitionFit: Tame means unexciting — a tame ending to a match — and the Tame is a Midlands river, so one word answers both halves.

entries.clue: 23 ...8 cooked food (4)

indicators.note: Cooked ingredients come out of the pan as something other than what went into it, so the letters are to be rearranged.

blocks.note: the answer at 8 down, four letters going into the pan

annotation.surface: Something cooked, to eat.
annotation.walkthrough: The dots carry the sentence on from the clue above, and 'cooked' is the only instruction in the pair — it does the work for both answers. The letters come from another entry, not from this clue's own words.
annotation.definitionFit: Meat is food in the oldest sense of the word — meat and drink meant anything eaten — as well as the flesh on the plate.
